summary: This proposed standard defines how to represent configuration data, state data, RPC parameters and notifications defined in YANG as JSON text. It gives the rules so that data modeled in YANG can be exchanged in a format familiar to web developers.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language network devices use to describe their configuration and state. This RFC says how to write that same information as JSON text, so a web service and a network device can exchange it without either side needing XML.

questions: how to represent yang data in json
how is yang data encoded in json
why are 64 bit integers strings in yang json
how is the empty type encoded in json
subtitle: Rules for writing YANG configuration and state data as JSON text.

tldr.problem: YANG defines only an XML encoding for the data it models, so management protocols that want to speak JSON had no standard way to write the same data as JSON text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives rules for naming, for the shape of each kind of data node, and for the JSON value that each YANG type becomes, following the restricted I-JSON profile where possible.
tldr.outcome: Configuration data, state data, RPC and action parameters and notifications can all be exchanged as JSON, and apart from anyxml and schema-less anydata the JSON can be converted to and from the XML encoding when the data model is available.

today: RFC 7951 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a JSON Encoding for YANG Data
sections.content:
The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) uses XML to encode data in its content layer. Other management protocols may want to use other encodings while still benefiting from YANG as the data modeling language. The RESTCONF protocol, for example, supports two encodings: XML with the media type application/yang.data+xml, and JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) with the media type application/yang.data+json.

The YANG 1.1 data modeling language defines only an XML encoding of data trees, meaning configuration data, state data, the input and output parameters of Remote Procedure Call operations or actions, and notifications. This document defines the rules for encoding the same data as JSON text.

The rules apply to every kind of data tree, and with the exception of the anydata encoding they also apply to YANG 1.0. The top-level structure in JSON-encoded data is always an object, and instances of YANG data nodes are encoded as members of that object, that is, as name and value pairs.

Unlike XML element content, JSON values carry partial type information, because a JSON value is a number, a string or a boolean. The encoding is defined so that this information is never in conflict with the data type of the corresponding YANG leaf or leaf-list. Except for anyxml and schema-less anydata nodes, a JSON-encoded data tree can be mapped to the XML encoding and back, although such conversions need the YANG data model to be available.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG describes the shape of network data, and this document describes how to write that data as JSON. One JSON object holds everything, and each part of the model becomes a member of it.

sections.title: Names and Namespaces
sections.content:
A JSON object member name MUST be in one of two forms. The simple form is identical to the identifier of the corresponding YANG data node. The namespace-qualified form prefixes the data node identifier with the name of the module in which the node is defined, separated by a colon. The ABNF production is member-name = [identifier ":"] identifier. The name of a module determines the namespace of all the data node names defined in it, and a node defined in a submodule uses the name of the main module it belongs to.

The namespace-qualified form MUST be used for all members of a top-level JSON object, and also whenever the namespace of the data node differs from that of its parent. In all other cases the simple form MUST be used. So in a model with a single module, the top-level container carries the module prefix while the leaves inside it do not. If the container is augmented from a second module, the augmented leaf does carry a prefix, because it comes from a different module than its parent.

Explicit namespace identifiers are sometimes needed when encoding values of the identityref and instance-identifier types, where the same namespace-qualified form is used. For an instance-identifier, the leftmost, top-level data node name is always namespace-qualified, and any subsequent name is qualified when the node is defined in a module other than its parent. The same rule holds for names inside predicates.
sections.plainLanguage: A name gets a module prefix when it comes from a different module than its parent, and the top level is always prefixed. Inside one module, plain names are enough.

sections.title: How Each Kind of Node Is Encoded
sections.content:
A leaf is a name and value pair, where the value is a string, a number, the literal true or false, or the special array [null], depending on the leaf's type. A container is a name and object pair, with the container's child data nodes as members of that object. A leaf-list is a name and array pair, where the array holds scalar values of that type. A list is a name and array pair, where the array elements are JSON objects. Character encoding MUST be UTF-8.

The ordering of array elements follows the same rules as the XML encoding, so the ordered-by properties of YANG MUST be observed. The order of members within a list entry, however, is arbitrary, because JSON objects are unordered collections, unlike XML list entries where the keys come first in a specified order.

An anydata node holds an arbitrary set of nodes that otherwise appear as normal modeled data, and it is encoded like a container, as a name and object pair. A data model for the content may or may not be known at runtime, and without one, converting the instance to XML may be impossible. Because the content must still be modelable by YANG, the JSON text inside must be valid I-JSON, all member names must satisfy the member name production, any array must hold either only unique scalar values or only objects, and the null value is only allowed in the single-element array [null] that encodes the empty type.

An anyxml instance is a name and value pair whose value must satisfy I-JSON. Apart from instances of data nodes, a JSON document MAY contain special object members whose name starts with the at sign, used for purposes such as encoding metadata; the syntax and meaning of those members are outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of node has its own shape: a leaf is a value, a container is an object, a leaf-list is an array of values, and a list is an array of objects. The order of entries in an array matters, but the order of the fields inside an entry does not.

sections.title: How YANG Types Become JSON Values
sections.content:
The type of the JSON value depends on the type of the data node. The integer types int8, int16, int32, uint8, uint16 and uint32 are represented as a JSON number. The int64, uint64 and decimal64 types are represented as a JSON string holding the lexical representation of the YANG type. This special handling of 64-bit numbers follows the I-JSON recommendation to encode numbers outside the IEEE 754 double-precision range as strings.

The string type is a JSON string, and the boolean type is the literal true or false. The enumeration type is a JSON string, one of the names assigned by enum statements. The bits type is a JSON string holding a space-separated sequence of the names of the bits that are set. The binary type is a JSON string holding the base64 encoding of arbitrary binary data. A leafref value uses the same rules as the type of the leaf it refers to.

An identityref value is a string holding the name of an identity. If the identity is defined in a module other than the leaf holding the identityref, the namespace-qualified form MUST be used; otherwise either form is allowed. The empty type is represented as [null], an array whose only element is the null literal, which counts as an atomic scalar value for this purpose. It was written that way rather than as a plain null so that empty leaves work in programming languages where a null member value is treated as if the member were absent.

A union value is encoded as the value of any of its member types, and the type information carried by the JSON syntax must also be taken into account when validating it. So for a union of uint16 and string, the JSON value 13.5 is an error, because JSON says it is a number and it is not a valid uint16, while the value "1" is a string. An instance-identifier value is a string analogous to its lexical representation in XML, with the namespace rules described earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each YANG type has one fixed JSON shape. Wide numbers and decimals become strings so that no precision is lost, and the empty type becomes a one-element array holding null.

sections.title: Following the I-JSON Profile
sections.content:
I-JSON is a restricted profile of JSON that guarantees maximum interoperability for protocols that use JSON in their messages, whatever JSON encoders and decoders the implementations happen to use. The encoding defined here follows the constraints of that profile as closely as possible, so that a wide range of existing JSON parsers can be used.

Four properties are guaranteed. The character encoding is UTF-8. Member names within the same JSON object are always unique. The order of JSON object members is never relied upon. And numbers of any type supported by YANG can be exchanged reliably.

The encoding deviates from I-JSON in exactly one place, the representation of the binary type. To stay compatible with the XML encoding, base64 is used, while I-JSON recommends base64url instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules follow a stricter JSON profile so that any parser can read the data. The only departure is that binary data uses base64 rather than the URL-safe variant.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines an alternative encoding for data modeled in YANG, so it adds no security issues beyond those discussed in Section 17 of the YANG 1.1 specification.

It defines no mechanism for signing or encrypting YANG-modeled data. Under normal circumstances, data security and integrity are guaranteed by the management protocol in use, such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. Where that is not the case, external mechanisms such as PKCS number 7 or the JSON Object Signing and Encryption specifications need to be considered.

JSON processing differs from XML processing, so JSON parsers can suffer from different kinds of vulnerability than XML parsers. To minimize these new risks, software on the receiving side SHOULD reject all messages that do not comply with the rules of this document and reply with an appropriate error message to the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security rules of its own. It does warn that JSON parsers have their own failure modes, so a receiver should refuse anything that does not follow these rules.
